name: bluewater-tales-93-102
lines: This is the oldest customer complaint in the world.
It is three thousand seven hundred years old. And it is furious.
The city of Ur. Around seventeen fifty BC.
A man named Nanni pays a merchant for fine copper.
The merchant is Ea-nasir. The copper shows up. It's junk.
So Nanni sends a servant to get his money back.
Ea-nasir sends him home with nothing. More than once.
So Nanni does what angry customers do. He writes a review.
Except there is no phone. He presses every word into wet clay. Front and back.
He writes that he has been treated with contempt. And he wants his money back, in full.
And here's the best part. Ea-nasir kept it.
Archaeologists found it in his house. With more complaints, from more customers.
Today it belongs to the British Museum. And the whole internet knows his name.
Not for his copper. For one unhappy customer.
A complaint used to take clay and a long walk. Now it takes ten seconds.
So fix it while it's still a conversation. Before it becomes a record.
Two thousand years ago, a man in Pompeii put ads in his own floor.
His name was Scaurus. He sold fish sauce.
Romans put fish sauce on everything. And his was the one to get.
How did they know? Because he told them. Everywhere.
Every jar had his name painted on it. From the workshop of Scaurus.
Some even carried a slogan. The flower of fish sauce.
Then he went further. In the hall of his own house, he laid a mosaic.
Four giant jars. In stone. With his name on them.
Every guest who walked in was walking across his ad.
He became the biggest fish sauce name in Pompeii.
Then the volcano buried the city. And the floor survived.
Two thousand years later, we still know what he sold. And that he said it was the best.
He never had a logo designer. He just put his name on his work. Every single time.
Your truck. Your shirt. Your invoice. Your yard sign. Is your name on all of it?
Why is a baker's dozen thirteen? Because bakers were terrified.
England. Twelve sixty six. Bread is life. And the king has a new law.
Every loaf must weigh what the law says. Exactly.
Sell a loaf that's too light, and you pay for it.
A fine. Your oven smashed. Or the pillory, in front of the whole town.
Here's the problem. Bread is not exact.
It rises. It dries. It shrinks in the oven. No baker could be sure.
So the story goes, bakers found a way to sleep at night.
Order twelve loaves. They gave you thirteen.
One extra. Just in case. Their insurance against the law.
Customers did not see insurance. They saw a baker who gives more.
More than seven hundred years later, we still call it a baker's dozen.
Nobody remembers the law. Everybody remembers the extra loaf.
So give a little more than you promised. It's the cheapest marketing there is.
This sign is on your street right now. And it means blood.
The red and white barber pole. You have walked past it your whole life.
Eight hundred years ago, a barber did not just cut hair.
He pulled your teeth. He set your bones. And he drained your blood.
It was called bloodletting. People thought it cured almost everything.
You gripped a pole, so your veins stood out. And he made the cut.
Then he wrapped your arm in white bandages.
And when he was done, the story goes, he hung the bandages outside to dry.
Red and white. Twisting in the wind. Around the pole.
Nobody needed to read. Everybody knew what that shop did.
The bloodletting stopped centuries ago. The sign never did.
That's what a good sign does. It tells a stranger what you do, in one second, without a word.
Now look at your truck. Would a stranger know?
New York, eighteen fifty four. A man stands on a platform, high above a crowd.
It hangs from one rope. And he tells his assistant to cut it.
His name is Elisha Otis. And he has a problem.
He has invented a brake that stops an elevator from falling.
It works. He knows it works. And almost nobody is buying it.
Because in eighteen fifty four, everybody knows one thing about elevators.
The rope breaks. And you die.
He could say it's safe a thousand times. Nobody would believe him.
So he stops talking. He takes a spot at the world's fair. And he climbs on.
Up he goes. The crowd looks up. The axe comes down.
The platform drops. A few inches. And stops.
All safe, gentlemen, he calls down. All safe.
After that day, the orders came. And cities started growing up, instead of out.
He did not win with a better claim. He won with proof people could watch.
So stop telling customers you're good. Film the job. Show them.
In eighteen seventy two, a salesman in Chicago mailed farmers one sheet of paper.
It listed a hundred and sixty three things. With prices. No pictures.
His name was Montgomery Ward. And his idea sounded crazy.
Send your money to a stranger, in a city you have never seen.
And he'll send your goods to the nearest railroad station.
Farmers loved the prices. But they had been cheated before.
How do you trust a man you will never meet?
He knew the answer was not a better ad.
In eighteen seventy five, he printed one sentence in the catalog.
Satisfaction guaranteed, or your money back.
Now the risk was his. Not theirs.
The single sheet became a book. By the eighteen nineties, it was nearly a thousand pages.
And three million people were on his mailing list.
Your customer is in the same spot. A stranger. Their home. Their money.
So take the risk off them. And put your promise in writing.
Why does a tire company hand out the most famous restaurant award on earth?
France. Nineteen hundred. Two brothers make tires. Their name is Michelin.
They have one big problem. Almost nobody drives.
There are fewer than three thousand cars in the whole country.
And the people who own one barely go anywhere. So the tires never wear out.
The brothers do not print an ad that says, buy tires.
They print a little red book. And they give it away.
Maps. Where to find fuel. How to change a tire. Where to sleep. Where to eat.
Thirty five thousand copies. Free. In a country with three thousand cars.
The book was not about tires. It was about going somewhere.
People drove further. Tires wore out. And they bought more.
More than a century later, chefs lose sleep over that book.
It started as help. Free, useful help, for the exact people they wanted as customers.
So what do your customers need to know? Write it down. And give it away.
In thirteen ninety three, the King of England made it illegal to sell ale without a sign.
Not a custom. A law. No sign, and they took your ale.
Here's why. Ale had to be tested. By an official ale taster.
Best job in the country. One problem. He could not find the ale houses.
They looked like every other house on the street.
So King Richard the Second gave the order. Brew ale to sell, and you hang out a sign.
And there was a catch. Almost nobody could read.
So the signs were pictures. A white stag. A red lion. A crown.
Meet me at the Red Lion. Even if you had never read a word in your life.
Six hundred years later, those pictures are still the names.
The Red Lion. The White Hart. The Crown. Still pouring.
A law about inspectors made some of the oldest brand names in Britain.
Because a picture is faster than words. And it sticks.
Can someone find your business without reading a thing? One mark. One colour. One look.
This is the oldest printed ad in the English language. And it ends with a plea.
Westminster. About fourteen seventy seven.
William Caxton has just set up the first printing press in England.
He has printed a handbook for priests. Now he has to sell it.
So he prints something new. A slip of paper, no wider than your hand.
And he puts it up where priests will see it. On walls. On doors.
It says what the book is. It says the printing is good and correct.
It says where to come. His shop, at the sign of the Red Pale.
And it says the price is good. Good cheap, in his words.
What you get. Where to go. Why it's worth it. In seven lines.
Then one last line. In Latin. Please do not remove this notice.
Five hundred and fifty years later, two copies have survived.
Most ads today forget what his remembered. What is it. Where do I go. Why you.
Read your last ad. Are all three in it?
For a hundred years, every business in town fought over one yellow book.
And the story goes, the yellow was an accident.
Cheyenne, Wyoming. Eighteen eighty three. A printer is making a telephone directory.
Halfway through, he runs out of white paper.
So he grabs what's on the shelf. Yellow.
People noticed. The yellow pages were easy to find.
Three years later, a man named Reuben Donnelley made it official.
A book of businesses. Sorted by what they do. On yellow paper.
And for the next century, that book was where customers looked.
Businesses named themselves triple A, just to be first on the page.
If you were not in the book, you did not exist.
Then the book moved. Into a phone. Into a search box.
The yellow is gone. The rule is not.
Be where people look. Today that's your Google listing. Is yours claimed? And is it right?
